title: Serving runtime architecture, kernel scheduling, profiling and runbooks
author: Maya Thompson
content:
Summary:
This consolidated playbook describes Redwood Inference's serving runtime architecture, kernel scheduling model, profiling and benchmarking playbooks, known issues, and on-call/runbook procedures. It is intended for engineers on the runtime, infra, and SRE teams and for any cross-functional work that changes runtime scheduling, batching, or kernel behavior.

Goals:
- Provide a single reference for architecture and ownership
- Give step-by-step profiling and benchmarking procedures for performance investigations and PR validation
- Define scheduler configuration targets, safety limits, and rollout guidance
- Document runbooks for common incidents and links to deeper runbooks/metrics

Audience and ownership:
- Primary: eng-serving-runtime (architecture, kernels, scheduling, profiling)
- Secondary: eng-sre (capacity/SLOs), eng-infra (deploy/packaging), product (release coordination)
- Owner: Runtime Platform (engineering)

1) Architecture overview
High level: The serving runtime is the inference execution stack used across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments. Major components:
- Frontend (API/gateway): request validation, auth, per-request routing, rate limiting
- Router/service layer: model routing, policy decisions (latency/cost/region), fallback handling
- Runtime workers: GPU processes executing kernels, with per-worker KV cache and session management
- Batch coordinator: aggregates in-flight requests into micro-batches; maintains dynamic batching windows
- KV cache service (optional): shared prefix cache for identical request prefixes across workers
- Metrics and tracing: token-level latency, queue time, kernel occupancy, tail-percentiles

Design principles:
- Predictable latency (p99 targets per class), graceful degradation (fallbacks), and cost-sensitivity (batching & quantization)
- Pluggable scheduler: policy driven (latency-first, throughput-first, cost-aware) with safe defaults

2) Kernel scheduling and resource model
Scheduling goals and constraints:
- Minimize p99 latency while achieving target throughput on GPU pools
- Maximize GPU utilization via continuous batching and kernel fusion where possible
- Avoid thrashing and memory OOMs by enforcing per-worker memory budgets and KV cache caps

Primary scheduler concepts:
- Worker slot: single logical inference execution context on a GPU (may host multiple micro-batches concurrently depending on kernel)
- Batch window: configurable duration (default 6ms) used to collect requests for a micro-batch
- Priorities: emergency, low-latency, standard, bulk; scheduler enforces priority pre-emption rules
- Kernel selection: chosen based on model, quantization profile, sequence length percentile, and batch size

Key scheduler configuration (example):
- default_batch_window_ms: 6
- max_batch_size: 64 (model dependent, enforced per model profile)
- memory_headroom_ratio: 0.12
- low_latency_cutoff_ms: 80 (requests with historical latency < cutoff prioritized to low-latency queue)

3) Profiling playbook (when investigating performance regressions)
Quick checklist:
1. Confirm the symptom: increased p50/p95/p99, higher GPU mem usage, or reduced throughput. Note the time window and affected model(s).
2. Reproduce on staging: use perf-harness with representative traffic (see Benchmarking suite below).
3. Collect traces: enable debug trace for 5 min for affected model/route (trace tags: trace_id, request_ts, batch_ts, kernel_choice, queue_ts).
4. Gather metrics: GPU occupancy, kernel latencies, batch sizes, queue lengths, KV cache hit rate, scheduler decisions.
5. Run kernel-level profiler: use nvprof/nsys or internal micro-bench to get kernel-level timings and memory footprints.
6. Compare against baseline: compare against last known-good run using the same input distribution.

Detailed steps:
- Step A: Snapshot runtime config (kubectl get configmap serving-runtime-config -o yaml) and archive under /tmp/profile-<date>.yaml.
- Step B: Run perf harness for 10m at 2x normal traffic: ./perf_harness --model gpt-xx --seq 1024 --qps 200 --duration 600 --seed traffic-2026-03-04
- Step C: Collect traces from tracing service: /api/traces?start=<ts>&end=<ts>&service=runtime
- Step D: Kernel profiler (on a dedicated node): sudo nsys profile --output=profile-<id> --stats true --force-overwrite --trace=nvtx --target-process <pid>
- Step E: If batch windows are low, try increasing default_batch_window_ms by +2ms and re-run to measure latency vs throughput tradeoffs.

Root-cause checklist (common causes):
- Sudden model change or new quantized model pushed without matching kernel profile
- Hot code path causing serialization before batching (locks around cache/KV access)
- Memory regression in model weights or activation allocations
- Scheduler misconfiguration or new priority rules causing starvation

4) Benchmarking suite and verification
Purpose: Standardized harness used to validate changes (PRs, kernel updates, scheduler changes) before rollout. All PRs affecting runtime must include a perf check where applicable.

Components:
- perf_harness: synthetic load generator supporting configurable seq lengths, prompt distributions, temperature, qps profiles, and token-emission rates
- microbench: executes isolated kernels to measure latency and memory at single-batch sizes
- scale_test: k8s job to spin a dedicated test pool and execute a full-production-scale workload for 30–60 minutes

Standard scenarios (example):
- Latency smoke: 50 qps, seq 256, p95 < 120ms for small models
- Throughput validation: 200 qps sustained for 30m, target GPU occupancy > 70%
- Long sequence: seq 2048, verify KV cache hit-rate > 30% and p99 acceptable

Example perf_harness command:
./perf_harness --model redwood-7b-q --seq 1024 --qps 150 --duration 1800 --workload-file workloads/realistic-chat.json --emit_tokens 10000

Acceptance criteria for changes touching kernel or scheduler code:
- No p99 regression > 10% vs baseline for targeted models and sequences
- GPU memory usage within 5% of baseline
- Batch size distribution not skewed towards smaller batches unless intentionally changed

5) Release notes and rollout guidance
When releasing changes to kernels or scheduler:
- Create a release note that includes: change summary, expected perf impact, models affected, baseline numbers, rollback steps. Link to perf_harness results.
- Canary rollout: 5% -> 25% -> 100% over minimum 24h windows with automated checks at each step.
- Automated checks must include: p50/p95/p99, error-rate, avg batch size, kernel error logs, memory OOMs.
- If any check fails, automatic rollback to previous config and page the on-call.

6) Known issues (operational)
- Issue: Occasional p99 spikes when KV cache becomes thrashable during mixed short/long sequence workloads.
  Mitigation: enforce prefix eviction policy, increase memory_headroom_ratio to +0.05 for affected pools, schedule segmentation by sequence-length profile.
- Issue: Kernel selection regression after quantized kernel update causes 3–7% latency increase for seq 512.
  Mitigation: roll back kernel, run microbench to identify offending kernel, add kernel ABI tests.
- Issue: Lock contention on shared cache causing queue delay ~10–40ms under bursts.
  Mitigation: move to sharded cache design and increase batch_window_ms temporarily.

7) Runtime runbooks (on-call)
Priority incidents and steps:
- Symptom A: Global p99 increase for a model family
  1) Check deployments: kubectl get pods -n serving --selector=model=<model> -o wide
  2) Check queue / batch metrics: grafana -> Serving Runtime -> Batch windows, Batch size distribution
  3) Check recent releases: /releases/runtime (last 24h) for kernel/scheduler changes
  4) If linked to a release, trigger rollback and increase canary to 0 for that change.
  5) If not, capture traces + run perf_harness against staging to reproduce.

- Symptom B: Memory OOMs on GPU workers
  1) Identify affected nodes: kubectl describe pod <pod> and check dmesg / kubelet logs
  2) Temporarily cordon node and scale up spare capacity pool
  3) Lower memory_headroom_ratio by 0.02 on worker pool config and redeploy
  4) Collect heap / profiler outputs for postmortem

- Symptom C: Batch starvation for low-latency customers
  1) Check priority queues; confirm low-latency queue not starved by bulk traffic
  2) If starved, increase low_latency_weight in scheduler config (example: low_latency_weight: 1.5) and monitor

8) Diagnostics and observability checklist
Essential dashboards and alerts:
- Serving Runtime Overview: p50/p95/p99 by model and region
- Batch Metrics: avg batch size, batch window ms, queue length by priority
- Kernel Metrics: kernel latency histograms, kernel error rates, occupancy
- Memory & OOM: per-worker GPU memory used, eviction counts
- Tracing: sample traces for slow requests (link from Grafana panels)

Critical alerts (examples):
- p99_above_slo (p99 > SLO for 10m) -> page on-call
- gpu_oom_count > 1/hour -> SEV2, investigate immediately
- kernel_error_rate > 0.5% in 5m -> channel alert, start rollback plan

This document collates content from across the team wiki. For deep dives:

- Profiling tools usage: confluence/eng-serving-runtime/serving-runtime-profiling-benchmarks-2026-03-30

Appendix A — Config reference (table):
- SLO targets: small-models p99 <= 120ms, medium-models p99 <= 250ms, long-seq p99 <= 800ms
- default_batch_window_ms: 6
- max_batch_size: model-specific (configured per model profile)
- memory_headroom_ratio: 0.12
- kv_cache_shards: 16

Appendix B — Example runtime config snippet (YAML):
server:
  default_batch_window_ms: 6
  low_latency_cutoff_ms: 80
  max_concurrent_batches_per_worker: 4
scheduling:
  policy: cost_aware
  low_latency_weight: 1.0
  bulk_weight: 0.6
limits:
  memory_headroom_ratio: 0.12
  max_batch_size_default: 64

Appendix C — Quick commands
- Snapshot config: kubectl get configmap serving-runtime-config -n serving -o yaml > /tmp/serving-config-$(date +%s).yaml
- Run perf harness: ./perf_harness --model <model> --seq <len> --qps <n> --duration 600
- Fetch traces: curl -sS "https://tracing.api/services/runtime/traces?start=<ts>&end=<ts>" > traces.json
